description: How the internal engineering roles relate to each other around the platform: who sets direction and budgets, who serves whom with foundations and guardrails, and which feedback loops keep golden paths honest.

relationTypes.name: Commercial
relationTypes.description: Internal service agreements and adoption commitments between engineering groups

relationTypes.name: Operational
relationTypes.description: Day-to-day delivery, guardrail enforcement, and platform-backed service provision

relationTypes.name: Financial
relationTypes.description: Infrastructure cost allocation, budgets, and showback

relationTypes.name: Information
relationTypes.description: Technical direction, standards, friction feedback, and posture reporting

relations.name: Sets delivery priorities and flow targets
relations.description: Directs what the team ships next and holds engineers to delivery-flow targets, relying on platform flow metrics rather than status meetings to see where work stalls.

relations.name: Steers engineers onto golden paths
relations.description: Sets the team's technical direction and points engineers at the sanctioned platform paths, templates, and safe defaults instead of bespoke infrastructure choices.

relations.name: Escalates platform friction
relations.description: Reports where service bootstrap, environments, or pipelines fall short of the golden path so the tech lead can push fixes into platform standards rather than local workarounds.

relations.name: Enforces release guardrails
relations.description: Applies policy-as-code gates on builds, artifacts, and deployments so engineers release with security and reliability controls checked automatically instead of by ticket.

relations.name: Requests policy exceptions
relations.description: Raises time-boxed exception requests when a guardrail blocks legitimate work, giving the reliability and security lead an auditable queue instead of shadow bypasses.

relations.name: Agrees reliability and readiness standards
relations.description: Negotiates SLOs, production-readiness criteria, and incident-review outcomes with tech leads so reliability standards land in service designs, not just in postmortems.

relations.name: Provides data and ML workload foundations
relations.description: Serves product engineers with specialist data and ML runtimes, pipelines, and tooling built on the shared platform's environments, artifact stores, and delivery machinery.

relations.name: Aligns specialist workloads with controls
relations.description: Shares data and ML workload patterns and their extra needs (GPUs, data access, model artifacts) so guardrails cover specialist pipelines without blanket blocking them.

relations.name: Allocates infrastructure budgets
relations.description: Sets the team's infrastructure and environment spend envelope using platform cost showback, and expects engineers to keep workloads inside it.

relations.name: Surfaces cost and capacity tradeoffs
relations.description: Translates platform cost and capacity data into concrete tradeoffs (rightsizing, environment tiers, architecture changes) that the engineering manager can plan and fund.

relations.name: Commits teams to specialist platform services
relations.description: Agrees internal service commitments with the data and ML platform area — which offerings the product teams adopt, at what support tier, and against which shared cost allocation.
